questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer:
Geneva is one of the best places in the world to study international law. Especially since the Certificate in Transnational Law program, which is offered at the faculty of law at the University of Geneva, allows you to take up to two courses at the Graduate Institute of International and Development Studies, one of the highest-ranked universities in the field of international law. 

Of course, the nature in and around Switzerland is incredibly appealing. You can do endless, astonishing hikes and skiing trips with the mountains and lakes all around the country, and it is really easy to go to the neighbouring countries, Italy and France, as well.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: My stay has been amazing. Really nice people from all around the world, and Switzerland has so much to offer. The only downside is how expensive it is here.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I think it's been fairly easy. The only thing is that a lot of the information available on the UNIGE website, as well as information that you get from old school letters, is in French. That makes it a bit more complicated, but with all the translation tools available, for example AI assistants, I've managed without knowing much French.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: All the incoming exchange students had an intro session on the Friday before the start of the semester, where we got all the information we needed about things like application for residence permit, opening a bank account (necessary for receiving the SEMP grant), applying for courses and so on.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: It would've been nice if all of the relevant pages for exchange students on the university's website were translated into English

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I was offered a spot through the Bureau des Logements (BLOG). I stayed at the Les Epinettes residence, which was really nice! Only a 10-minute walk from Uni Mail, where I had all of my classes and most of my exams, and nice apartments. I highly recommend applying for both BLOG and the Cité. Every place has it's upsides and downsides.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I think you miss out a little bit on some of the social stuff going on at the Cité Universitaire. They have very nice facilities such as common areas for chilling or studying, sports facilities such as tennis, padel, football, gym, and volleyball, which is nice. However, you do have access to most of it even though you don't live there.

Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: There is a limited registration period, but the staff at uni are kind to inform you about it so that you don't miss it. You have the possibility to try out different courses before making the final registration. First you register for the courses, and then later, you register for the exams, which is binding.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The staff, including some of the professors, helped explain the process. You help each other among the other exchange students.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: At UNIGE, I got all the courses that I wanted, but I didn't get the two courses at the Graduate Institute that I applied for, even though I had 5 priorities. I ended up only getting one course at the Graduate Institute, which was my last priority.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Keep the deadlines in mind!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I haven't gotten my grades at the time of writing this, but overall, I think it's quite doable. It depends a lot on the individual course, though. In some courses, you have close to no readings to do prior to the classes, but in others, it's quite extensive. In my experience, the workload at the Graduate Institute is quite a lot bigger than that at the UNIGE, but I don't think the level is much different. I think the level is comparable to the level of the English courses taught at the UCPH.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It varies a lot from course to course. In some of the courses, the classes are recorded. Some of them require you to show up to the classes. Some of them use a participation bonus system. The course I had at the Graduate Institute, International Investment Law, had participation bonus, but also the other way around, so you would get deducted if you didn't show up or participate, when you were on the panel. You were assigned with two classes where you were expected to be extra well prepared as part of the "panel".

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Comparative Methodology: Tort Law
International Intellectual Property Law
Internet and IT Law 
Economic Analysis of Law 
International Investment Law (at the Graduate Institute)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
While you're here, I think it's worth it to go for the Certificate in Transnational Law. This means that you have to take a Comparative Methodology course. Besides that, I really liked Internet and IT Law. Especially one of the two professors, prof. Alberini, was excellent. International Intellectual Property was nice, but quite demanding. 
I highly recommend going for one or two courses at the Graduate Institute as part of the Certificate in Transnational Law program.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: In general, the prices in Switzerland are high. That wasn't too unexpected.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: I was pleasantly surprised that public transport in the entire canton of Geneva is free for students up to the age of 25. As a young student you can also get a group day pass (up to 4 people) valid for the entire country for only 80 chf, which is incredibly cheap compared to the normal price. Unfortunately, I've been too old to get the good deals, so it's been quite expensive for me. If you're too old for the benefits, I'd recommend getting the half-fare travel pass as soon as possible, if you see yourself going on trips around Switzerland.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Geneva is a fairly small city, so if you're looking for a place to go clubbing several times a week, I don't think this is the right place for you. But it was more than enough for me here, and the prices set a kind of natural limit.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: The ESN network hosted many different activities throughout the semester. There's so much going on, and the activities available vary from club nights to sports, to hikes, to skiing, to sightseeing.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Hiking, skiing, visiting the smaller towns around Switzerland. The incredible nature in and around Switzerland is what makes Geneva stand out in my opinion.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Hiking, skiing, visiting the smaller towns around Switzerland. The incredible nature in and around Switzerland is what makes Geneva stand out in my opinion. 

It's a no-brainer to go to France and maybe also, depending on what you like, Italy, Spain, Germany.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: The overall vibe is a lot like Copenhagen, I think. And it's very international here, so I'd say it's quite easy.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Make an effort during the first few weeks. That really helps you in the long run. I think the welcome week hosted by the ESN was a really great way of getting to know many people.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: The fact that the supermarkets are only open till 19.00 and closed on Sundays is annoying. But you get somewhat used to it along the way.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: If you want to try out your French, people are very kind and understanding. And almost everyone knows English, so if you get stuck in a sentence, you can (almost) always switch to English.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Put in the effort in the beginning. Not only socially, but also in terms of getting your bank account set up, getting your residence permit etc. It's way better to just get it out of the way compared to having it hanging over your head for several months. 
Show up to classes. For me, it was a good way to maintain a normal every day life, and it's nice to see your classmates on a regular basis without having to plan something every time. And you have plenty of time doing fun stuff in the weekends, since almost everyone has Fridays off and I also had Mondays off.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: As a Dane, who is also too old for the public transport benefits, it's been nice to have a bike here. I bought one on Facebook Marketplace and will sell it again, but you can also rent one for your entire stay. Kind of like Swapfiets.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Getting to know all sorts of amazing people from all around the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The troubles of getting a bank account, residence permit, etc. The entire administrative system is based on physical letters back and forth.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
